rationale: B wins by a nose because it keeps the same three usable lanes while making fewer unsupported leaps. A's "someone who ran systems inside Tesla Energy" and "software is the cheap fix being tried" start writing facts the update did not provide; B's "the angle only exists once the fund is named and a partner states the thesis on record" is the cleaner editorial posture. B still overcooks "breaking the local grid," but it is less likely to walk the founder into a reporter's fact-check buzz saw.
gaps_in_A: "someone who ran systems inside Tesla Energy" invents a founder role. The update only says ex-Tesla Energy and ex-NREL, not what either founder did there.

"Community-solar grids are hitting a load-balancing wall" and "software is the cheap fix being tried" assert a market problem and cost comparison not in the update. The proof note is good, but the headline is still too hot.
"the fund's name (you have it; I don't)" assumes the founder has a named lead fund ready. The supplied update only says a climate-focused seed fund.

The refused angle "Three utilities are already paying Verdano" is tagged as hallucinated, but the update says three paying utility customers in pilot. The real problem is unnamed, unproven pilots, not the payment fact.
gaps_in_B: "keep community solar from breaking the local grid" is punchy but overstates the supplied fact. The update says cut grid strain, not prevent grid breakage.
"ex-Tesla Energy commercial grid experience plus ex-NREL research credibility" adds role color the facts do not support. Confirm teams, titles, and dates before that survives a pitch.

The category angle needs more than a named utility and pilot mechanic. It also needs independent evidence, or at least another market example, showing this is a category and not one startup's funding narrative.

"the other two need the named fund and a named utility first" undersells the proof gap. The category story also needs evidence of actual community-solar grid strain before a serious trade reporter bites.
